newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish court delays Gonzalez "dirty war" ruling.
newsitem.headline: Spanish court delays Gonzalez "dirty war" ruling.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court left open on Thursday the possibility it will question former premier Felipe Gonzalez about a 1980s "dirty war" on ETA separatists, a scandal which helped oust his Socialist party from power after 13 years.

Over-ruling one of its own members, the court told Supreme Court justice Eduardo Moner that he first had to hear an appeal by families of the victims against his earlier decision that Gonzalez need not be probed.

Only after the appeal has been heard will the court make its final ruling on whether to summon Gonzalez -- either as a witness or a suspect -- in a case which continues to cast a long shadow over Spanish politics.
Court sources said that the appeals process could take around a month.

Moner decided last April, shortly after Gonzalez lost power in general elections, that there was no hard evidence linking the Socialist Party leader to the 1983-87 illegal campaign of bombings and killings in which 27 people were killed.
He subsequently refused to consider any appeal, arguing that it was not legally admissable. The Supreme Court, however, did not agree.

"The judge (Moner) took a decision on the matter and we have taken a different view. There was a difference of interpretation (of the law)," said Supreme Court Judge Joaquin Delgado after the full court deliberated for about an hour and a half.
The once-charismatic Gonzalez, 54, has been rendered largely ineffective in opposition to the conservative Popular Party government by the continued rumblings of the "dirty war" scandal.

Former security chiefs and a disgruntled former Basque region leader of his own Socialist party accuse him of authorising the illegal action against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) rebels. A third of those killed had no connection with ETA.
Gonzalez was compelled to call an early election in March after the "dirty war" allegations and corruption scandals discredited his government.
A former Socialist interior minister, Jose Barrionuevo, is already on trial before the Supreme Court on charges of creating and funding the anti-ETA death squads.
The Basque separatists campaign for independence has killed about 800 people since 1968.
